new_statements.quote: Pitch and length are not phonemically relevant in Waskia. Word stress is not fully predictable but strong tendencies have been observed, as follows: [3.3.1.1 Words other than verbs.] Stress is predominantly on the first syllable in two- and three-syllable words, and on the second syllable in four-syllable words. [...] [3.3.1.2 Verbs] Stress in verbs is to a great degree predictable. Future tense: Stress is penultimate. [...] In words of three and more syllables primary and secondary stress are hard to distinguish. However there is always a stress (either primary or secondary) on the final syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) codes Waskia as fixed-strict FINAL stress (final stress, domain quote Ross & Paol 1978:2 'in general.. stress falls on the last syllable'). The dedicated SIL phonology says stress is not fully predictable and, for non-verbs, predominantly INITIAL in 2-3-syllable words and on the second syllable in 4-syllable words; verbs are penultimate in the future tense. The only overlap with the catalog's final-stress claim is non-future verbs of 3+ syllables, where a (primary or secondary) stress always sits on the final syllable, which is what Ross's 'verb (i.e. on its subject-tense-mood suffix)' describes. Different placement AND different type (lexical with tendencies vs fixed-s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No tone or length contrast. Word stress is 'not fully predictable' but has strong positional tendencies split by word class. Non-verbs: initial stress in 2- and 3-syllable words (in open-final disyllables 'almost always' initial, /pu're/ 'thunder' the only known exception), second syllable in 4-syllable words; a second syllable beginning with /r l s g/ (in trisyllables /r l/) often attracts the stress (/ba'ras/ 'star', /ga'lep/ 'light', /ba'rarem/ 'reef'), with counter-examples (/'welang/ 'oil', /'bugung/ 'bee') and inflecting body-part/kin terms unaffected. Verbs: future tense penultimate (/nama'nako/ 'we will go', unchanged by a clitic or loss of the final vowel); other tenses: disyllables usually initial (/'balam/), 3+ syllables always carry a primary or secondary stress on the FINAL syllable with alternating stresses before it (/'nama'man/ 'they went', /ge'rago'so/), five+ syllables 'final syllable stress with stress on preceding alternate syllables' modulated by infixes and stem length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: in verbs of three or more syllables 'primary and secondary stress are hard to distinguish', but there is 'always a stress (either primary or secondary) on the final syllable'; the preferred rhythm in long verbs is final stress plus alternating stresses on preceding syllables (/'baga-'laga-'san/ 'they kept on staying', /ba'taga-ruka'san/); some infixes such as /-gi'lingi-/ always keep their own stress (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: Non-verbs: /pu're/ 'thunder' (only open-final disyllable with non-initial stress); onset-driven second-syllable stress /ba'ras/, /pu'rong/, /ga'lep/, /pu'lut/, /sa'sal/, /ku'sen/, /da'gor/, /ba'gun/, /ma'tangi/ 'outside', /ba'rarem/, /bu'lulu/, versus initial /'welang/, /'ka(u)sik/ 'dog', /'bugung/, /'wosasel/, /'bugulik/ (p. 26). Sec. 3.3.2 (p. 28): 'Very few contrasts for which there is no apparent reason have been found', listing /a'maru/ 'when' vs /'awila/ 'how many', /na'nawus/ 'daughter' vs /'naniwus/ 'our wives', /pu'lut/ vs /'welang/, /ba'gun/ vs /'bugung/ (near-contrasts, not true minimal pairs).
new_statements.identity_note: Barker & Lee's data are from Kaul village (Kaul I), northern Karkar Island, Madang Province, six months in 1976, c. 1000-word dictionary, language helper Bangsik Akus (Introduction, printed p. 1). Ross & Paol 1978 is the Waskia of Ross's co-author John Natu Paol; no dialect difference is claimed by either source, and the OPD gives the language's major villages as Kaul, Ungen and Keng, so both describe the same Karkar Island language rather than distinct varieties.

new_statements.quote: Stress in verbs is to a great degree predictable. Future tense: Stress is penultimate. /nama'nako/ 'we will go' A suffixed clitic does not change this stress, nor does the absence of the final vowel or syllable from the basic form [...] Other tenses: In two-syllable words the first syllable is usually stressed, e.g. /'balam/ 'he said' In words of three and more syllables primary and secondary stress are hard to distinguish. However there is always a stress (either primary or secondary) on the final syllable. [...] [3.3.2 Stress Contrasts] Very few contrasts for which there is no apparent reason have been found.

Its verb statement is the one place that partly matches the catalog's final-stress coding (final syllable of non-future 3+-syllable verbs always carries some stress), but the future tense is penultimate and non-verbs are predominantly initial, so the fixed-strict final coding does not hold for the language as a whole.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same manuscript as index 0 (third listing of SIL archive 31253). Verb half of the rule quoted here: future tense penultimate regardless of clitics or apocope; non-future disyllables initial; non-future 3+-syllable verbs always have a primary or secondary stress on the final syllable, with alternating stresses before it; a handful of unexplained stress contrasts among non-verbs (p. 28).
new_statements.secondary_stress: As index 0 (p. 27): alternating secondary stresses before a final stress in long verbs; certain infixes keep their own stress.

readall_conflicts: The three listed works are one and the same 40-page SIL manuscript (Barker & Lee, 'A tentative phonemic statement of Waskia', SIL archive 31253; index 1 is a dead duplicate URL, index 2 repeats index 0's URL), so there is no disagreement among the works opened. There is a direct disagreement between that manuscript and the catalog's deciding source: Ross & Paol 1978:2 (PL B-56, sec. 1.1, says Waskia has 'weak, non-contrastive stress.. In general, however, stress falls on the last syllable' of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, which the catalog coded as fixed-strict final. Barker & Lee (1976 Kaul data) say stress is 'not fully predictable', give a short list of unexplained contrasts, and place it predominantly on the FIRST syllable of 2-3-syllable non-verbs, the second syllable of 4-syllable non-verbs, and the penult in future-tense verbs; only non-future verbs of 3+ syllables always carry a (primary or secondary) final stress, which is plausibly what Ross heard on the subject-tense-mood suffix. Barker's 1992 Organised Phonology Data sheet (SIL 42492, held by the project, not in the works list) repeats the manuscript: 'Word stress is not fully predictable but strong tendencies have been observed. In two- and three-syllable words stress is usually on the first syllable, but can be also on the second syllable. The functional load of phonemic stress is very low' (p. 3). The two SIL sources agree with each other against Ross; Ross himself hedges ('in general', 'need…

audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed-strict' final (counts as exceptionless (the strict set), in the dominant set, final stress). reclassify as classification conflict (Ross & Paol 1978:2, hedged 'in general' final vs. the two dedicated SIL phonologies, which agree with each other against Ross), or, if the catalog resolves conflicts toward the dedicated phonology, as 'lexical' with strong positional tendencies (stress 'not fully predictable', low-functional-load contrasts; non-verbs predominantly INITIAL in 2-3-syllable words, second syllable in 4-syllable words, /r l s g/-onset second syllables often attract stress; verbs: future tense penultimate, other tenses disyllables initial, 3+ syllables always a stress on the final syllable with alternating stresses before it). the primary-stress rule should carry both statements; cite Barker & Lee n.d. [1976 data] sec. 3.3.1-3.3.2 pp.26-28 and Barker 1992 OPD p.3 alongside Ross 1978:2. Also fix the locator 'section 1.1 Phonology' -> 'section 1.1 General' and populate the empty top-level quote/cite/grade fields.

Deciding source is the standard and only published grammar (Ross & Paol 1978, PL B-56, grammar sketch), so the record rests on the best published description, and the classification (final stress, enclitics excluded, word domain) follows the text.
